title: VLT image of a double-detonation supernova
caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0509-67.5, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
credit: ESO/P. Das et al. Background stars (Hubble): K. Noll et al.

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Two concentric shells of blue sit inside a glow of orange in this image of SNR 0509-67.5. This spreading debris is all that is left of a star which blew up several centuries ago.

The colours are a chemical map. The data come from MUSE, the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer on ESO's Very Large Telescope, which can show where each chemical element lies. Calcium is shown in blue and hydrogen in orange.

The two calcium shells are the key finding. They indicate that the star died in a double detonation, exploding with two blasts rather than one. According to ESO, this is the first photographic evidence that stars can die this way. The two nested layers of calcium are read as the signature of those two blasts, preserved in the debris of the star as it spreads.

understand.summary: The VLT's MUSE instrument mapped individual elements in visible light: calcium is shown in blue and hydrogen (H-alpha) in orange, with background stars from Hubble.
understand.eye: MUSE separates the light of individual elements, something no eye can do, so this is a map of chemistry rather than a direct view.

explore: The background stars in the image come from Hubble data, while the chemical map of the remnant comes from the VLT. MUSE records a spectrum at every point, which is what allows each element to be pulled out and coloured separately.
alt: Two concentric blue shells inside an orange glow, surrounded by stars.
